title: India Warns Against Using Visa-Free Malaysia Entry to Find Jobs
excerpt: India's High Commission in Kuala Lumpur says it has seen a "noticeable increase" in travellers misusing the 30-day visa-free facility to seek work, warning of overstay, exploitation, detention and legal action.
body:
• India's High Commission in Kuala Lumpur has advised Indian nationals against using Malaysia's 30-day visa-free entry facility to seek employment.
  • The mission reported a "noticeable increase" in Indians arriving through the visa-free route to find jobs, many misled by agents making false employment promises.
  • The 30-day facility is granted for tourism and social visits only; using it for work violates Malaysian immigration rules.
  • Genuine tourists should carry a confirmed return ticket, hotel booking, Malaysia Digital Arrival Card submitted three days prior, and a passport valid for six months.

India's High Commission in Kuala Lumpur has issued a formal advisory warning Indian nationals against using Malaysia's 30-day visa-free entry facility to travel to the country in search of employment, cautioning that such attempts could lead to overstay, illegal immigration status, exploitation, detention and legal action.

The advisory, posted on X on Tuesday, flags a "noticeable increase in Indian nationals arriving in Malaysia using the 30-day visa-free facility, to seek employment." The mission said it has been alerting Indian nationals travelling to Malaysia on tourist visas against taking up employment.

Agents making false job promises

A central driver of the warning is the role of recruitment agents. "Many Indian nationals are misled by unscrupulous agents with false job promises, leading to overstay, illegal status, exploitation, detention and legal action," the advisory said.

"Many Indian nationals are misled by unscrupulous agents with false job promises, leading to overstay, illegal status, exploitation, detention and legal action."

— High Commission of India, Kuala Lumpur

The pattern — false overseas job offers followed by immigration violations and workplace exploitation — has been a recurring concern for Indian workers in Southeast Asia, with earlier advisories targeting similar rackets in countries such as Cambodia and Myanmar.

Visa-free entry does not permit employment

The High Commission stressed that seeking employment through the visa-free route is a clear violation of Malaysian immigration rules. The facility, which allows Indian passport holders to stay in Malaysia for up to 30 days, is "granted for tourism and social visits only" and does not permit employment.

Malaysia's visa exemption for Indian travellers remains in place until December 31, 2026, under its current immigration rules. The mission clarified that the exemption covers tourist travel alone — it is not a back-door route to the Malaysian labour market.

What travellers should do instead

The advisory is categorical: "Indian nationals are strictly advised not to travel to Malaysia for work/employment purpose without work permit or visa with reference (VDR)." Workers planning legal employment must obtain the appropriate employment documentation — including a valid work permit or a Visa With Reference — before travelling.

Genuine tourists, meanwhile, should carry valid and verifiable documentation to avoid immigration-related issues on arrival: a confirmed return air ticket, hotel booking details, proof of online submission of the Malaysia Digital Arrival Card (MDAC) at least three days before the scheduled arrival, and a passport with minimum six months' validity.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, the advisory is a reminder that Malaysia — home to one of the largest Indian-origin populations in Southeast Asia — runs a parallel labour system in which legal employment requires employer sponsorship and government approvals. Job-seekers tempted by easy entry should verify any offer through official channels and confirm visa sponsorship in writing before leaving India.

The High Commission's warning adds Malaysia to the growing list of destinations where fraudulent job-promising agents have put Indian travellers at legal and personal risk, and where the difference between a tourist entry and a work visa is the difference between a holiday and a detention cell.
